title: Establish the ASX IOMR candidate for semantic integrity, arbitration, and replay safety

changes.content:
# Protocol

ASX is an exchange and agreement protocol. Two agents use it to show that they named the same published meaning, started from the same authoritative state, and applied the same pinned rules. An observer checks the bytes. The protocol does not run an AI model, store an ontology, interpret a workflow, schedule work, or carry packets.

SCL is the modelling language for the requirements in `model/iomr`. The Python library does not import SCL, and agents do not need an SCL runtime to exchange a round record.

## Semantic integrity

<!-- anchor-intent-semantic-integrity -->

Independent agents agree the declared semantic references and the authoritative starting state before a consequential transition. Matching reference bytes means they named the same publication. It does not mean two models understood that publication in the same way.

<!-- anchor-model-semantic-agreement -->

Agent A offers a canonical decision tied to a semantic reference, a parent hash, and a successor hash. The semantic authority's publication is what the reference names. Agent B checks those bytes and can countersign the same decision bytes. A verifier checks the parent at the commit boundary. Any mismatch stops the exchange.

<!-- anchor-outcome-matching-references -->
<!-- anchor-rn-matching-references -->

A semantic reference in version 1 is the ASCII token `authority:identifier@frame+revision`. `references_match` is byte equality of the canonical token. Callers who need a snapshot digest put it in the revision slot or in the Mahalath extension. ASX does not fetch the snapshot.

<!-- anchor-outcome-pre-state -->
<!-- anchor-rn-pre-state -->

The commit checks the expected parent hash at the same boundary as the state change. A proposal whose parent is no longer current is `stale-parent`. The successor hash is 32 bytes supplied by the proposer and covered by the proposal commitment. ASX does not execute the successor. It binds the hash the agents declared.

<!-- anchor-outcome-joint-certification -->
<!-- anchor-rn-canonical-bytes -->

Joint certification means independent signatures over the same decision bytes from `docs/arbitration.md`. Different bytes are not the same decision. Duplicate JSON members are not a canonical form: the transcript is binary, and a JSON object presented as a transcript is `malformed-transcript`.

<!-- anchor-outcome-identical-validation-results -->
<!-- anchor-rn-identical-validation -->

Two implementations given the same round record produce the same transcript, closed-set digest, challenge, ranking, winner, and rejection codes, or the same halting code. The in-repository checker under `conformance/independent/` is a local cross-check of that rule. An implementation developed outside this repository is still outstanding.

<!-- anchor-outcome-fail-closed -->
<!-- anchor-rn-fail-closed -->

If the references differ, the parent does not match, the certificate does not verify, or the ranking is ambiguous, there is no state change and no effect. The library's illustrative stores keep a commit counter and an effect hook so tests can see that a rejection leaves both unchanged.

## Replay safety

<!-- anchor-intent-replay-safety -->
<!-- anchor-model-replay -->

Invalid, duplicated, stale, or unauthorised exchanges do not commit a second effect. The replay key is:

```text
SHA256("ASX/replay/v1" || 0x00
       || u32be(len(round_id)) || round_id
       || u32be(len(identity)) || identity
       || proposal_commitment[32]
       || parent_hash[32])
```

<!-- anchor-outcome-replay-detection -->
<!-- anchor-rn-replay -->

A store that already holds the key returns the original receipt with code `replay-receipt`. The illustrative file replay log reloads that key after a process restart on one node. That is not a replicated log.

<!-- anchor-outcome-atomic-rejection -->
<!-- anchor-rn-atomic -->

A halting rejection is returned as a `Rejection` with a normative code. The illustrative commit path runs the effect hook only after compare-and-swap succeeds. A rejection before that point does not call the hook and does not change the parent.

<!-- anchor-outcome-no-duplicate -->
<!-- anchor-rn-no-duplicate -->

A successful commit followed by a retry of the same key does not call the effect hook again. Two racing compare-and-swap operations on the illustrative memory store allow one successor.

<!-- anchor-outcome-recovery -->
<!-- anchor-rn-recovery -->

`IllustrativeJournal` records a prepare record, the new parent, and whether the demonstration effect hook has been marked done. Recovery after `after-apply` runs the hook once. Recovery after the done flag is set does not run it again. If the hook ran in the outside world and the done flag was not stored, recovery can call it again. External exactly-once delivery is not claimed. See `LIMITATIONS` in the package.

<!-- anchor-outcome-consistent-failure -->
<!-- anchor-rn-precedence -->

The rejection codes and their order are the list in `docs/arbitration.md`. The same malformed input produces the same code from the reference decoder and the independent decoder. Tests cover truncated transcripts, a JSON object used as a transcript, a little-endian length, an overflowing count, non-ASCII identities, and duplicate identities.

## What a round record contains

The JSON object accepted by `asx.evaluate` is a test and tooling record, not the normative transcript. The transcript is the binary encoding. Unknown JSON fields, including a transport nonce, are ignored. Fields that are present and malformed still fail closed: a bad admission sequence, a bad hex parent, or a bad asserted priority does not become a different winner.

The pure function does no I/O. Stores, ledgers, and HMAC keys are separate and illustrative unless a deployment replaces them with a system that actually has the property the class does not claim.

# Arbitration

<!-- anchor-intent-deterministic-arbitration -->

Conflicting proposals must produce one governed decision that another implementation can recompute from the authenticated round record. Message arrival order is not an input.

<!-- anchor-model-arbitration -->

The logical process is: proposal submission, authenticated admission, admission closure, canonical set construction, priority evaluation, tie-breaking, decision certification, authoritative commit, then audit and rejection handling. This chapter fixes the bytes for the middle of that process. It does not require a particular database, transport, or cryptographic library beyond SHA-256 and the encodings below.

<!-- anchor-model-policy-pinning -->

A policy steward publishes one policy revision. The round pins that revision's digest. Changing the policy starts a new round.

## Version

Canonicalisation version 1 is identified by the domain tags in this chapter. A round record whose `canonicalisation_version` is not 1 is `unsupported-version`. There is no second encoding, including JSON, that verifiers may accept as the transcript.

## Admission

<!-- anchor-rn-admission -->

A governed identity is authenticated by a proof over the submission binding. The identity string alone is not a proof. The binding is:

```text
"ASX/submit/v1" || 0x00
|| u32be(len(round_id)) || round_id
|| u32be(len(identity)) || identity
|| proposal_commitment[32]
|| parent_hash[32]
|| policy_digest[32]
```

<!-- anchor-rn-one-proposal -->

Each governed identity has at most one eligible proposal in a round. A durable sequencer assigns a strictly increasing admission sequence when the admission commits. The first successfully committed admission for that identity is authoritative. An identical retry, meaning the same identity, proposal commitment, parent hash, and policy digest, returns the original receipt and does not consume another sequence number. A distinct later submission from the same identity is `duplicate-submission`.

<!-- anchor-rn-fixed-context -->

The round identifier, parent hash, pinned policy digest, and admission rules stay fixed for the round. A submission after closure is `admission-closed`. It is recorded as deferred and is not inserted into the closed set. If the sequencer cannot allocate a sequence, the result is `sequencer-unavailable`. Client clocks, client sequence numbers, gateway arrival times, and a local observer's arrival order do not assign precedence.

The reference `IllustrativeMemoryAdmission` and `IllustrativeFileAdmission` classes demonstrate these rules in one process or one file. They are not a distributed linearizable sequencer.

## Canonical semantic proposal

A proposal commitment is SHA-256 over a length-prefixed semantic proposal. The semantic proposal is:

```text
"ASX/semantic-proposal/v1" || 0x00
|| u32be(len(semantic_ref)) || semantic_ref
|| u32be(len(operation)) || operation
|| u32be(len(content)) || content
|| successor_hash[32]
```

```text
proposal_commitment =
  SHA256("ASX/proposal/v1" || 0x00
         || u32be(len(semantic_proposal)) || semantic_proposal)
```

`content` is opaque bytes. Transport nonces, request identifiers, and receipt timestamps are not fields of this encoding. Text fields are the ASCII grammars below. Implementations do not Unicode-normalize. A value outside the grammar is rejected, so two different normalizations cannot both be accepted.

| Field | Grammar | Maximum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| identity, round id, policy revision | `[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._:-]{0,127}` | 128 bytes |
| semantic reference | `[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._:@+/-]{0,255}` | 256 bytes |
| operation | `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,128}` | 128 bytes |
| content | opaque bytes | 1,048,576 bytes |
| eligible entries | — | 1,024 |
| extensions | — | 16, payload 4,096 bytes each |

Integers are big-endian. `u32be` is unsigned. `i64be` is signed two's complement. A length that overruns the buffer, a count above the version-1 maximum, trailing bytes, or a domain mismatch is `malformed-transcript`.

## Canonical closed set

<!-- anchor-rn-transcript -->

Eligible entries are not stored in admission order. Each entry is:

```text
u32be(len(identity)) || identity || proposal_commitment[32] || i64be(effective_priority)
```

Entries are sorted by ascending unsigned `identity` bytes. Distinct identities need no secondary sort key. The transcript is:

```text
"ASX/closed-set/v1" || 0x00 || u32be(entry_count) || concat(sorted entries)
```

`S = SHA256(transcript)`.

<!-- anchor-rn-sequence-excluded -->

The admission sequence is authenticated in a separate admission receipt:

```text
"ASX/admission/v1" || 0x00
|| u32be(len(round_id)) || round_id
|| u32be(len(identity)) || identity
|| proposal_commitment[32]
|| parent_hash[32]
|| policy_digest[32]
|| u64be(sequence)
```

That sequence is not part of the eligible-set transcript, the closed-set digest, or the derived challenge. Replacing the sequence on an otherwise identical eligible set does not change `S` or the winner. Verifying who was admitted first requires the signed admission log. Ranking reproducibility does not prove that the admission was fair.

Duplicate identities are `duplicate-identity` and are detected before `S` is accepted. A non-grammar identity is `noncanonical-identity`. A non-grammar proposal field is `noncanonical-proposal`. These checks happen before a winner is selected. A verifier that sees them in a purported eligible set halts the round rather than dropping a different subset than another verifier.

## Derived challenge

<!-- anchor-outcome-ranking -->

```text
Q = SHA256("ASX/challenge/v1" || 0x00
           || u32be(len(round_id)) || round_id
           || parent_hash[32]
           || policy_digest[32]
           || S[32])
```

`Q` is a pure function of those inputs. Two implementations with the same authenticated inputs produce the same `Q`.

<!-- anchor-rn-grinding -->

`Q` is not independent randomness and it is not grinding resistance. A proposer who can guess the rest of the closed set can try semantic bodies offline and submit the body with the preferred tie digest. One admission per identity removes multiple admitted chances. It does not remove that offline search. This specification does not claim grinding resistance. The reference result field `grinding_resistance` is the string `unproven`.

## Priority and tie-breaking

<!-- anchor-rn-priority -->

Effective priority comes from the pinned policy and the proposal operation. A priority asserted by the proposer is not an input. If an authenticated record carries `asserted_priority` and it differs from the policy value, the round halts with `priority-untrusted`. An operation with no rule is `ineligible-operation`.

<!-- anchor-rn-tie -->

Among eligible entries:

1. Higher policy priority outranks lower policy priority.
2. For equal priority, compute `tie = SHA256("ASX/tie/v1" || 0x00 || Q[32] || proposal_commitment[32])`.
3. Select the minimum unsigned 32-byte tie digest.
4. If two entries in the winning priority class have the same tie digest, halt with `tie-collision`.

<!-- anchor-rn-collision -->

Do not break that tie with admission order, identity order, a clock, or "first decoded". Identity order is only a stable display order for the published ranking list after the winner is unique. A claimed commitment that does not match the semantic bytes is `commitment-mismatch`. Different semantic bytes with one computed commitment are `commitment-collision`. Both halt with no winner.

This tie digest replaces the earlier unchallenged rule that compared SHA-256 of the semantic body directly. ARB-05's "smaller digest" means this challenge-bound tie digest.

<!-- anchor-rn-single-mode -->

There is one arbitration mode. If no authoritative closure is available, the result is `arbiter-unavailable`. Implementations do not fall back to first arrival, first commit, or a local subset.

## Policy bytes

<!-- anchor-rn-frozen-policy -->

```text
"ASX/policy/v1" || 0x00
|| u32be(len(revision)) || revision
|| u32be(rule_count)
|| repeat, sorted by operation bytes:
     u32be(len(operation)) || operation || i64be(priority)
|| u32be(len(fairness)) || fairness
```

The policy digest is SHA-256 of those bytes. A declared digest that differs is `policy-stale`. Rule order in a JSON test record does not change the digest, because the encoder sorts rules. Duplicate rules are `policy-invalid`.

<!-- anchor-outcome-fairness -->
<!-- anchor-rn-fairness -->

`fairness` is empty or exactly `max-wins:<integer>` with no spaces and a value from 0 to 1,000,000. Empty means no extra schedule. Unknown fairness text is `policy-invalid`, not an invitation to invent a scheduler. `max-wins` requires an explicit prior-win map. A missing map is `policy-invalid`. A count greater than or equal to the cap is `fairness-violation` for the whole round, not a silent drop of one entry. Absent the directive, prior wins do not change ranking.

## Decision certificate

<!-- anchor-outcome-recorded-rejection -->
<!-- anchor-rn-rejection -->

A successful decision names one winner and a rejection for every other eligible identity. Rejection codes on a success are `lower-priority` or `higher-tie-digest`. They are sorted by identity for the certificate. Halting codes are not mixed into that list, because a halt has no winner.

Decision bytes, without the signature:

```text
"ASX/decision/v1" || 0x00
|| u32be(len(round_id)) || round_id
|| parent_hash[32] || policy_digest[32] || S[32] || Q[32]
|| u32be(len(winner_identity)) || winner_identity
|| winner_commitment[32] || i64be(winner_priority) || winner_tie[32]
|| u32be(rejection_count)
|| repeat, sorted by identity:
     u32be(len(identity)) || identity || u32be(len(code)) || code
```

The signature algorithm is not fixed by version 1. The reference HMAC-SHA256 helper is illustrative. A bad signature or a payload that does not match the recomputed decision is `certificate-mismatch`. A payload that is not this encoding is `malformed-certificate`.

<!-- anchor-outcome-recomputation -->
<!-- anchor-rn-recompute -->

A third party that receives the round record, the pinned policy, and the semantic bytes recomputes the transcript, `S`, `Q`, the ranking, the winner, and the rejection codes. Disagreement halts certification.

## Commit

<!-- anchor-outcome-one-successor -->
<!-- anchor-rn-selection -->
<!-- anchor-rn-commit -->

Selection does not change state. The selected successor is committed with compare-and-swap against the expected parent, or an equivalent serialisable check. A stale or competing parent is `stale-parent`. A caller who is not the certified winner is `unauthorized`. Losing proposals are not rebased onto the new parent. A second commit of the same replay key returns `replay-receipt` and does not run the effect again.

Two committers racing from the same parent produce at most one successful swap in a correct store. The illustrative memory store demonstrates that race inside one process. It does not demonstrate a distributed log.

## Failure precedence

The first matching check wins. Later codes are not reported once an earlier check has failed.

1. `unsupported-version`
2. `malformed-transcript`
3. `malformed-certificate`
4. `noncanonical-identity`
5. `noncanonical-proposal`
6. `duplicate-identity`
7. `commitment-collision`
8. `commitment-mismatch`
9. `ineligible-operation`
10. `priority-untrusted`
11. `policy-invalid`
12. `policy-stale`
13. `fairness-violation`
14. `closed-set-mismatch`
15. `extension-invalid`
16. `extension-critical-unknown`
17. `admission-unauthenticated`
18. `duplicate-submission`
19. `admission-closed`
20. `sequencer-unavailable`
21. `arbiter-unavailable`
22. `empty-closed-set`
23. `tie-collision`
24. `certificate-mismatch`
25. `unauthorized`
26. `stale-parent`
27. `commit-rejected`

Successful outcome codes, which are not halts: `lower-priority`, `higher-tie-digest`, `replay-receipt`, `committed`.

When a closure is missing, a partition hides the sequencer, a certificate is malformed, or the parent is disputed, the implementation refuses the transition. Progress is optional. An unauthorised or stale effect is not.

## Extensions and the transcript

<!-- anchor-rn-extensions -->

Extension envelopes are outside the closed-set transcript. A noncritical extension, known or unknown, must not change `S`, `Q`, or the winner. A critical extension with no enabled handler is `extension-critical-unknown`. An enabled handler that rejects the payload is `extension-invalid` and yields no winner. Handlers do not return a priority.

# Security

<!-- anchor-trust -->

ASX tells an observer what to recompute. It does not make the surrounding systems honest.

| Boundary | Trusted for | Not trusted for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Proposing agent | Submitting a semantic body it is willing to stand behind | Priority, time, arrival order, identity without a proof |
| Semantic authority | The published bytes named by a reference | How a model will interpret those bytes |
| Policy authority | The priority table and fairness directive inside the pinned digest | Changing a round that already pinned a digest |
| Admission sequencer | Which submission from an identity committed first | The ranking digest. Sequence is outside `S` and `Q` |
| Commit authority | Serialisable compare-and-swap against the parent | Executing the successor, or inventing a winner when closed-set digests disagree |
| Verifier | Recomputation from the authenticated record | Discovering facts that were not in the record |
| Extension handler | Shape checks for an optional profile | Priority, transcript bytes, or core ranking |

A network partition, a missing arbiter, or a missing sequencer stops new admissions and new commits. It does not authorise a local first-arrival decision.

<!-- anchor-grinding -->

The derived challenge is public and deterministic. An agent can evaluate alternative semantic bodies before admission and keep the one with the better tie digest. Deterministic tie-breaking can pass while a grinding-resistance claim fails. Version 1 does not add an after-closure entropy source. Do not describe `Q` as a random beacon.

Identical semantic proposals from two identities at the same priority halt with `tie-collision`. Falling back to admission order would put the sequencer's sequence back into the winner. The halt is deliberate. It can stall a round in which two agents proposed the same body. Safety is preferred to progress.

<!-- anchor-illustrative-stores -->

`IllustrativeHmacKey` is a test authenticator with a shared secret of at least 16 bytes. It is not a production signature, a PKI, or a statement that HMAC-SHA256 will be the eventual algorithm. Receipts signed with it show the shape of an authenticated admission. They do not show that a deployment's keys are managed.

`IllustrativeMemoryState`, `IllustrativeMemoryAdmission`, `IllustrativeMemoryReplay`, and their file and journal counterparts are single-process or single-node demonstrations. They use a lock or an atomic file replace. They do not provide distributed linearizability, crash safety under concurrent processes, or exactly-once external side effects. `LIMITATIONS` in the package says so, and a test fails if those flags are flipped without a corresponding demonstration.

The effect hook on the journal can run twice when a crash falls between the external side effect and the done flag. Callers that need exactly-once effects need an idempotent effect and a store this repository does not yet provide.

Unknown critical extensions fail closed. Unknown noncritical extensions are ignored and are excluded from the transcript, so they cannot be used to move a tie digest. A critical extension that is understood still cannot change priority: a handler returns no rank.

SHA-256 collision resistance is assumed for `commitment-collision`. The test for equal tie digests uses identical commitments, which any implementation can construct. It does not construct a SHA-256 collision.

No security audit of this repository has been performed. The CI `bandit` job is a static scan of the reference library, not a review of the protocol.

# Conformance

<!-- anchor-vectors -->

The published corpus is `conformance/vectors/v1/corpus.json`. Each positive case stores the round-record inputs and the transcript hex, closed-set digest, challenge, ranking, winner, and rejections. Those expected fields were produced only when `src/asx` and `conformance/independent/recompute.py` returned the same success object. Negative cases store the shared halting code.

Regenerate with:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=src python3 scripts/generate_corpus.py
```

The generator refuses to write a case on which the two computations disagree. `tests/test_corpus.py` loads the file and checks both computations again. Editing an expected digest by hand fails that test.

<!-- anchor-arb-cases -->

| Case | What is checked | Where it runs | Verification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ARB-01 | No closure, no first-arrival commit | illustrative store test | locally tested |
| ARB-02 | Late admission leaves the admitted set unchanged | illustrative admission test | locally tested |
| ARB-03 | A local digest that differs cannot match the authoritative digest | `check_closed_set` | locally tested |
| ARB-04 | Policy priority, not a self-declared priority | pure `evaluate` | locally cross-checked |
| ARB-05 | Equal priority, lowest tie digest, order does not matter | pure `evaluate` | locally cross-checked |
| ARB-06 | Claimed commitment alias halts | pure `evaluate` | locally cross-checked |
| ARB-07 | Mixed-priority permutations share digest and winner | pure `evaluate` | locally cross-checked |
| ARB-08 | One compare-and-swap wins a race | illustrative memory store | locally tested |
| ARB-09 | Selection without commit leaves state and effects unchanged | illustrative store | locally tested |
| ARB-10 | Losing successor against the old parent is `stale-parent` | illustrative store | locally tested |
| ARB-11 | A revised policy does not rewrite a pinned round | pure `evaluate` | locally cross-checked |
| ARB-12 | Same rule as ARB-03 for competing local sets | `check_closed_set` | locally tested |
| ARB-13 | Replay returns the receipt and does not repeat the effect | illustrative replay log | locally tested |
| ARB-14 | Independent checker recomputes the winner | both implementations | locally cross-checked |
| ARB-15 | Only an explicit `max-wins` cap is enforced | pure `evaluate` | locally cross-checked |
| ARB-16 | Noncritical Deborah payload ignored; critical unknown halts | pure `evaluate` | locally cross-checked |
| ARB-17 | Transport nonce is not a ranking input | pure `evaluate` | locally cross-checked |
| ARB-18 | Identity byte order, including case | pure `evaluate` | locally cross-checked |
| ARB-19 | Shared reject codes for encoding traps | both decoders | locally cross-checked |
| ARB-20 | Parent mutation changes `Q`; sequence mutation does not | pure `evaluate` | locally cross-checked |
| ARB-21 | One winner of a same-identity race; file reload returns the receipt | illustrative ledgers | locally tested |
| ARB-22 | Different bodies move the tie digest; resistance stays `unproven` | pure `evaluate` | locally cross-checked |
| ARB-23 | Permutations agree on transcript, `S`, `Q`, ranking, winner, rejections | both implementations | locally cross-checked |

"Locally cross-checked" means the second computation lives in this repository and does not import `asx`. It is not an implementation written by another party. That external check is outstanding.

The pure cases are also in the corpus. The store cases are not represented as distributed traces. Their tests would pass on a single machine even if a real deployment double-committed.

<!-- anchor-historical-missing -->

`conformance/historical/STATUS.md` records the search for T01 and T13–T22 and for the earlier 1,024-case fuzz corpus. Those artifacts were not found. No historical run is claimed. The seeded fuzz in `tests/test_fuzz.py` is a new 1,024-draw check that the reference and the independent checker agree, including on random garbage transcripts. It is not the missing corpus.

## Requirement index

The requirement statements live in the SCL proposal under `.scl/proposals/`. This table names the tests that exercise them. It is not a second copy of the requirements. `TRACEABILITY.md` is generated when a trusted reviewer commits the model. That commit has not happened.

Every row is partial. The reference behaviour has local tests. Distributed linearizability, production signatures, external exactly-once effects, and an outside implementation do not.

question.Question: Does the derived challenge resist offline semantic grinding?
question.Context: Q is a public function of the round, parent, policy digest, and closed-set digest. A proposer can try semantic bodies before admission.
question.Blocks: any statement that version 1 provides grinding resistance

question.Question: What durable distributed sequencer commits admission exactly once?
question.Context: The reference admission classes demonstrate one process or one file. They do not show distributed linearizability.
question.Blocks: a production claim of distributed admission linearizability

question.Question: Will an implementation written outside this repository recompute the published vectors?
question.Context: The second checker in conformance/independent does not import the reference package and was written in the same effort.
question.Blocks: the independent-verification status of the published vectors

question.Question: Which production signature algorithm will authenticate admission and decisions?
question.Context: Version 1 fixes the signed bytes and uses an illustrative HMAC helper. It does not choose a production signature.

question.Question: Where are the historical T01, T13-T22, and 1024-case fuzz artifacts?
question.Context: A search on 2026-11-24 did not recover those bodies. The new seeded fuzz is not that corpus.
question.Blocks: any claim that the historical conformance cases were executed

question.Question: How will an external effect be exactly once when the completion flag is missing?
question.Context: Journal recovery can run an effect again when the effect happened and the done flag was not stored.
